newsitem.title: YEMEN: Aden port revival to start soon - officials.
newsitem.headline: Aden port revival to start soon - officials.

text.p: Dredging in Aden harbour is about to begin in the first tangible sign of work aimed at restoring the port to its position as a key staging post on the route from Europe to Asia, project executives said on Monday.
Revival of the port is an important element of the Aden Free Zone, a $500 million project to make Yemen's economic and commercial capital a major cargo trans-shipment hub.

The dredger is due to leave Singapore on Thursday and arrive on April 3 for 15 weeks of work scooping out sufficient seabed sand to enable the world's largest container carriers to call, officials said.
Then it is scheduled to shift to Salalah in Oman, further along the Indian Ocean coast, where U.S. developer Sealand is building a competing trans-shipment centre.

The Aden project is being driven by the Yemen Investment and Development Company (YEMINCO), an international consortium which includes Saudi investors of Yemeni origin as well as Saudi and U.S. development firms. Meneren Corporation of the United States is in charge of implementation.

Aden aims to deepen its navigation channel to 16 metres (52 feet) from a maximum of 12 metres now so it can offer facilities and fast turnaround times for the largest carriers now plying shipping routes from Europe through the Suez Canal and the Red Sea to Southeast Asia, Australia and East Africa.

"This will see Aden for the next 10 to 15 years," port development project manager Roy Facey told Reuters. "Aden has much to offer that will definitely encourage investors to come in. But there is a difference between interest and commitment and now they are showing commitment."
Reyad Nader, acting general manager for free zone investment projects, said dredging would show that Aden was serious about redevelopment.

"We're not joking here. It's a very serious business. By using Aden as an international hub instead of Gulf ports, international shipping companies can save at least three days. At a cost of $60,000 a day for the new jumbos of the seas, that's a big savings," he said.
"This should reduce the prices both of imported raw materials and exported finished goods," he said.

The new super-carriers, the first of which began service a year ago, carry 6,000 standard 20-foot equivalent unit (TEU) boxes and are set to transform the shipping industry as they bear more goods faster to world markets.

Aden's revival is a direct challenge to its regional rivals -- Saudi Arabia's Red Sea port of Jeddah and the Gulf ports of Dubai and Jebel Ali in the United Arab Emirates, which are dredged to shallower draughts.

Time was when Aden, one of the world's largest protected natural harbours, was an important staging post for shipping between Europe, the Mediterranean and Asia. Some 7,000 vessels called each year during its heydey in the 1950s and 1960s.
But war and domestic political uncertainty drove the trade elsewhere.
The closure of the Suez Canal for eight years after the 1967 six-day Arab-Israeli war ended Aden's role as a bunkering port for large vessels.
And an era of intense political rivalry between the once royalist north and Marxist south left Yemen in a state of instability that led to civil war as recently as 1994.

Aden, Britain's only colony in Arabia, was developed as a coal bunkering depot for ships carrying mail between Britain and the jewel in its imperial crown, India. It became the Arabian peninsula's most prosperous port of call.

With Yemen's only oil refinery and major port, it was designated as the economic and commercial capital of the unified country under a 1990 agreement on the merger between the Yemen Arab Republic in the north and the People's Democratic Republic of the Yemen in the south.
